scene.testo: Three German prisoners walked away from an American work crew in the Maine woods, carrying a compass made from a sewing needle and a peach can lid. Their goal was Argentina. A single Maine winter ended the plan in five days.
How do three young men, with no boat, no papers and no English, plan to cross an ocean? And why did they believe a frozen wilderness would let them go?
The answer begins on a frozen lake, with a sleeping guard. But the real danger was not the guard, or the manhunt that followed. It was what waited in the forest itself.
The date was March 7th, 1945. The place was Spencer Lake, in the North Woods of Maine. A crew of German prisoners of war was cutting ice, watched by one American guard.
The guard sat down under a fir tree and fell asleep. Three prisoners looked at each other, at the guard, and at the forest. Then they walked quietly into the trees.
They were Franz Keller, age 18, Horst Schlueter, age 19, and Anton Gabe, age 20. Boys, really. They had been soldiers of a collapsing army, and now they were prisoners a very long way from home.
They carried snowshoes they had built themselves. They carried knives, hoarded sugar, and a stolen map. And they carried that compass, a magnetized needle balanced on the tin lid of a peach can.
To understand how they got there, we have to go back to 1944. America held hundreds of thousands of German prisoners, and it had a serious problem at home: not enough men.
The young men of Maine were overseas. Yet the paper mills still needed pulpwood. Wartime America ran on paper, from ration books to the boxes that carried ammunition to the front.
So the prisoners were sent to the woods. Maine took in nearly 4,000 of them. The main camp stood at Houlton, near the Canadian border, with branch camps scattered across the state.
One branch camp stood at the north end of Spencer Lake, in a township called Hobbstown, west of Moosehead Lake. The Hollingsworth and Whitney paper company built it for 250 men.
It had 22 buildings, barbed wire and guard towers. In July 1944, 250 prisoners arrived by train at Bingham and rode the rest of the way in. By March, the camp held 310.
The nearest public road was 12 miles away. Remember that number. It matters later, because the isolation was the real fence. The wire was almost an afterthought.
Life there was not what a German soldier expected from an enemy prison. Under the Geneva Convention, prisoners were fed like American soldiers and paid for their labor in camp coupons.
They cut pulpwood all day. Evenings brought classes, music and sports. Across Maine, farmers and foremen were surprised by how hard the prisoners worked, and some came to respect them.
Still, a prison in the woods is a prison. And the camp commander, Major William Marshall, more or less dared his prisoners to try to escape. Three of them decided to accept.
They prepared all winter. They saved food from their rations and hid sugar under their clothes. They shaped snowshoes from boards and rail ties, with harnesses of leather belts and stovepipe wire.
On the work detail they had axes, and they made knives. From a French Canadian woodcutter they got a map. And then came the compass: a sewing needle, magnetized with an electrical coil.
The plan sounded simple. Walk about 100 miles to the coast. Board a freighter. Sail to Argentina, a country still friendly to Germany, and wait out the war in the sun.
On March 7th, the ice-cutting crew went out onto the lake. The guard sat down under his fir tree and slept. Keller, Schlueter and Gabe simply walked away into the forest.
Nobody noticed until evening roll call. Major Marshall called for help. By the next morning, about 30 men had arrived: state police, the sheriff, game wardens and the FBI.
They brought bloodhounds. It became one of the largest manhunts in Maine history. Three planes flew low over Spencer Lake for two days, looking for tracks, smoke, anything at all.
They found nothing. The forest had swallowed three men without a trace. So what was happening out there, beneath the pines, while the whole state searched for them?
The escapees were learning what the Maine woods are in March. They moved at night and slept by day, in shelters dug from the snow and roofed with pine boughs.
The snow was deep. The nights were well below freezing. And the stolen map and the peach can compass could not show them the thing that was about to stop them.
Rivers. Spencer Stream and the Dead River lay across their way. In March, beneath thin ice, the water runs black and fast. Three men on homemade snowshoes could not cross.
So they walked along the water, looking for a way over. And the rivers turned them where the rivers wanted them to go. The forest was steering the escape now, not the compass.
On the third day of the search, the sheriff deputized a man named Bill Hall. Hall was a hermit. Since 1932 he had lived alone in an old trapper's cabin in those woods.
He avoided people, and publicity even more. But he knew that country better than any warden. He had once tried to shout a warning to the Germans in their own language. It came out as, tie your shoes.
Now he studied the map and thought about the rivers. Men on foot, without a boat, could not cross them in March. They would have to follow the water downstream. And downstream led to one place.
That place was West Forks, a small logging settlement about 30 miles from the camp. Go to West Forks, Bill Hall told the wardens. The wardens listened.
On March 12th, 1945, five days after the escape, two Maine game wardens found a makeshift lean-to near West Forks. Inside were three cold, hungry German prisoners.
The wardens took their axes and marched them to a nearby country store, to wait for the army. They had covered about 30 miles of their 100. Argentina was exactly as far away as ever.

When the army questioned them, the answers surprised everyone. Nobody had mistreated them. One said Major Marshall had challenged them. Another simply dreaded another summer of mosquitoes and black flies.

Franz Keller spent three weeks in solitary confinement at Houlton. Then he took a correspondence course in astronomy from the University of Maine. The war ended that May, and the Spencer Lake camp closed in April 1946. In 1957 he returned, as an engineer, and helped build America's road to the moon.

descrizione:
In March 1945, three young German prisoners of war walked away from a work crew in the Maine woods with a compass made from a sewing needle and a peach can lid. Their goal was a ship to Argentina. A Maine winter, two frozen rivers and a hermit's guess ended the plan in five days.

This WWII documentary follows the Spencer Lake escape: the prisoner of war camps in Maine, the pulpwood labor program, one of the largest manhunts in state history, and what the escapees told the army afterward. One of them later worked on the Apollo program.
